quote: Wahrscheinlich Dreiecke auf der elliptischen Riemannschen Fläche.
english: Probably triangles on the elliptic Riemann surface.
topic: Hilbert extends an idea from spherical functions (Kugelfunktionen) to algebraic functions, Riemann surfaces, automorphic functions and the Lamé differential equation, and examines the conformal map given by the quotient of two integrals, with a footnote on the inverse of an integral involving $P_n$.

triage.modern_statement: Take the Lamé equation in Weierstrass form, w'' = (n(n+1)℘(z) + B) w, on the elliptic curve (torus) C/Λ. Its singular point is z = 0, where the exponent difference is 2n+1. Let f = w1/w2 be the quotient of two independent solutions (the Schwarz map, or developing map). Hilbert's guess appears to be that f is a conformal map which divides the elliptic Riemann surface into triangles bounded by circular arcs, much as the Schwarz map of the hypergeometric equation tiles the sphere into circular triangles in the classical spherical-function (P_n) case. In modern language: describe the geometric structure that f induces on the torus, i.e. a spherical metric (or a flat or translation structure) with one cone point of angle 2π(2n+1), and its decomposition into triangles. The note is short, so this reading is an interpretation and may not be exactly what Hilbert meant.
triage.answered_by: No single paper settles this exact one-line remark. The surrounding question was worked out in two stages. First, classically: the Schwarz–Klein theory of quotients of solutions as conformal maps onto circular polygons, including Klein's work on Lamé functions around 1890 and his pullback theory for Lamé equations with finite monodromy. I found no source on Klein's Lamé papers themselves; the search only reached secondary sources on his pullback theory. Second, in modern work: Eremenko, Gabrielov, Mondello, Panov and Tarasov (about 2015–2023) describe the developing map w1/w2 of the Lamé equation as a spherical metric on the torus with one conic singularity of angle 2π(2n+1), and they decompose it into triangles ('balanced flat singular triangles' and spherical polygons). Chai–Lin–Wang and Lin–Wang studied the same objects through the mean field (Liouville) equation and modular forms.

evidence.claim: The developing map of a spherical metric on a torus is f = w1/w2, the quotient of two independent solutions of the Lamé equation with the Weierstrass ℘-function and an accessory parameter.

Degree-m Lamé functions correspond one-to-one to translation structures on the torus with one conic singularity of angle 2π(2m+1). The paper analyses these structures using 'balanced flat singular triangles' and applies the result to spherical metrics with one conic singularity on a torus.
The moduli space of spherical tori with one conical point is described explicitly, answering a question of Chai, Lin and Wang.

Klein's pullback theory, which grew out of Schwarz's classification of circular triangles, applies to Lamé operators with finite projective monodromy: such operators are rational pullbacks of hypergeometric (Schwarz-triangle) operators.
Lamé equations with finite monodromy are treated through Schwarz triangles, Klein's pullback and spherical geometry on tori (2024).
Work continues on counting spherical metrics with one conical singularity on tori, building on Chai–Lin–Wang and Lin–Wang.

triage.why: The remark is a single tentative sentence. It fits the classical picture: Schwarz showed that quotients of solutions of second-order Fuchsian equations map onto circular triangles, and Hilbert seems to be carrying this over from the spherical-function case to the Lamé equation on an elliptic curve. The geometry of that quotient map on the torus was later worked out in detail, first by Klein and his pullback theory and recently in the spherical-metric and translation-structure literature, which explicitly breaks the torus into triangles. So the question as I read it has been answered and the area is still very active. It is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Confidence is low because I can't confirm what Hilbert meant by 'triangles' (spherical, flat or hyperbolic) or which integral quotient he was mapping. I also found no source that refers to this diary note.
